summary: Defines a mechanism that lets a DNS client be notified asynchronously when records change, rather than polling the server. This helps when records change frequently, such as for service discovery, without needing a high polling rate.

eli5.summary: Instead of checking the mailbox every minute, the mail carrier rings your doorbell. DNS can now ring when something changes.

questions: how to get notified of dns changes without polling
how do dns push notifications work
what port does dns push use
subtitle: Lets a DNS client subscribe to record changes over a long-lived TLS connection instead of polling for them.

tldr.problem: DNS is efficient for relatively static data, but when records change often the only option is polling, and there is no way for a client to be told asynchronously that something changed.
tldr.mechanism: A client opens a DNS Stateful Operations session over TLS over TCP, sends SUBSCRIBE messages for a name, type and class, and the server sends PUSH messages that add or remove records, until the client sends UNSUBSCRIBE or closes the session.
tldr.outcome: Clients get the same results as sufficiently rapid polling, more efficiently. If no subscription can be set up, they fall back to polling at a limited rate.

facts.label: Polling fallback
facts.value: At least min(900 s, TTL + 2 s)

today: RFC 8765 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2020, and neither obsoleted nor updated by another RFC according to the unit metadata. It builds on DNS Stateful Operations in RFC 8490.

sections.title: Why Push Instead of Poll
sections.content:
Polling can burden DNS servers at many levels of the network. A publish/subscribe model can deliver more timely notifications of changes with reduced CPU usage and lower network traffic.

The guiding principle is that a client using DNS Push Notifications receives the same results it could get via sufficiently rapid polling, only more efficiently. So the rules for which records match a subscription are the same as for a DNS query: names compare case-insensitively, and a CNAME matches any type.

Multicast DNS already announces changes to a link-local group. DNS-based Service Discovery (RFC 6763) across a wide area using Unicast DNS needs an equivalent. An earlier deployed solution, DNS Long-Lived Queries (RFC 8764), was UDP-based and reimplemented TCP-like state management in user space. This document instead uses DNS Stateful Operations (RFC 8490) over TLS over TCP, so it does not reinvent TCP features.
sections.eli5: Asking 'did anything change?' over and over is tiring for everyone. It is better to say 'tell me when it does' once and wait.

sections.title: Sessions, Transport and Subscription Limits
sections.content:
A client connects to the right Push Notification server for a record set and sends DSO messages naming what it cares about. The server for a zone is any server that can generate correct change notifications for a name: a primary, secondary or stealth name server. Supporting DNS Update and Push on the same server is OPTIONAL, and standard DNS queries MAY be sent over the same session.

Clients MUST use DSO running over TLS over TCP (RFC 7858). TCP gives return reachability and avoids state-overload by spoofed sources, and TLS is REQUIRED on every connection.

Push has a cost, so clients MUST NOT recklessly create too many subscriptions. A subscription should be active only while there is a valid reason, such as an on-screen display, and SHOULD be cancelled as soon as that need ends. A client SHOULD NOT routinely keep subscriptions open 24 hours a day just to keep a list warm. A session with an active subscription is not idle, but the DSO keepalive interval still applies. Servers can limit subscriptions, and clients may open sessions to alternate servers for the same zone.
sections.eli5: You should only ask to be notified about things you are looking at right now, and stop asking when you look away.

sections.title: Discovering the Push Server
sections.content:
The client first opens a DSO session to its normal recursive resolver on TCP port 853 and requests a subscription. If that works, the resolver subscribes upstream on the client's behalf and relays results. If the resolver lacks DSO support the session setup fails. If it has DSO but not Push, it returns the DSO error code DSOTYPENI (11). If it cannot subscribe for a name it should return SERVFAIL.

When that fails, the client discovers the server directly:

  • Send an SOA query for the full name, then strip one leading label at a time until an SOA appears in the Answer or Authority section. A single-label name means a configuration error and the client gives up.
  • Query the SRV record _dns-push-tls._tcp.<zone>, where the zone is the owner name of the SOA. If the zone offers Push, this record MUST exist. Its target and port say where to connect.
  • With several SRV records, use priority (lowest first) and weight to choose the order of servers.

Each new subscription SHOULD repeat discovery, reusing an existing session to the same server, and the client MUST respect DNS TTLs so repeated discovery is mostly answered from cache.
sections.eli5: To find who rings the doorbell for your street, you ask up the chain: first your neighbor, then the block, then the city, until someone says it is them.

sections.title: SUBSCRIBE Request and Response
sections.content:
A SUBSCRIBE request is a DSO message with the standard 12-byte DSO header and the SUBSCRIBE Primary TLV (type 0x0040). The DNS OPCODE is 6, the four count fields are zero, and the data holds exactly one NAME, TYPE and CLASS. The MESSAGE ID must be unique among the client's active operations on the session, and the server echoes it in the response.

Subscriptions on a session MUST be unique; a duplicate is a fatal error and the server forcibly aborts the connection. Wildcards are not supported: an asterisk matches only a literal asterisk. Subscribing to records the server does not yet know is not an error, and the server MUST NOT return NXDOMAIN. When TYPE or CLASS is 255, it means ALL, so the server MUST send updates for all matching changes.

The response's RCODE says whether the subscription was accepted. On an error the server SHOULD add a Retry Delay Additional TLV, and the client should not retry against that server right away. Existing subscriptions on the session stay in effect.
sections.eli5: Subscribing is like giving the mail carrier a note: 'ring me when anything arrives for this name.' The carrier writes back yes or explains why not.

sections.title: PUSH Updates
sections.content:
After a subscription is accepted, the server sends PUSH messages (type 0x0041). If the answer set was already non-empty, an initial PUSH follows the SUBSCRIBE response immediately. PUSH is unidirectional: its MESSAGE ID is zero and the client does not reply. A client MUST NOT send PUSH.

Each PUSH holds one or more change notifications that look like resource records, and the TTL field tells the client what kind of change it is:

  • TTL from 0 to 0x7FFFFFFF: add the record. A TTL of 0 means keep it while the subscription is active and discard it when the subscription ends.
  • TTL 0xFFFFFFFF: remove that individual record.
  • TTL 0xFFFFFFFE with RDLEN zero: a collective removal of a whole RRset, or all RRsets for a name in a class, or in all classes.

Any other TTL value is silently ignored. A change that affects several subscriptions produces just one PUSH. Servers SHOULD encode changes compactly, batch immediately available changes, and use DNS name compression. A PUSH MUST NOT exceed a DNS message length of 16,382 bytes; larger sets are split across messages.

While a subscription is active, stored TTLs are not decremented, and the client does not need to poll to confirm a record is still there. Clients silently ignore pushes for subscriptions they just removed, because UNSUBSCRIBE and PUSH can cross in flight.
sections.eli5: The doorbell rings with a note: 'a new card arrived' or 'this old card was taken away.' You keep your list up to date without leaving your seat.

sections.title: UNSUBSCRIBE, RECONFIRM, Closing and Polling Fallback
sections.content:
To cancel one subscription, the client sends a unidirectional UNSUBSCRIBE (type 0x0042) whose data is the 2-byte MESSAGE ID of the original SUBSCRIBE. It may be sent before the SUBSCRIBE response arrives, and servers MUST silently ignore an UNSUBSCRIBE that matches nothing. Closing the session cancels all subscriptions. The client should do an orderly TLS close with a close_notify alert and then a TCP FIN, since a TCP RST can lose data.

A client that suspects stale data, such as an SRV record whose target does not respond, can send RECONFIRM (type 0x0043) naming one record. A Discovery Proxy then re-checks using Multicast DNS. On other servers the operation is undefined and SHOULD just get NOERROR. If the record is gone, normal PUSH messages inform all interested clients.

If a client cannot get a subscription at all, it may fall back to polling. The interval between queries for the same name, type and class SHOULD be at least the minimum of 900 seconds or two seconds more than the TTL of the answer RRset, and before each re-query the client should try to subscribe again.
sections.eli5: You can cancel a notification at any time, or hang up the phone and cancel them all. If the doorbell is broken, you check the mailbox yourself, but not too often.

sections.title: Security and TLS
sections.content:
The Strict Privacy profile for DNS over TLS (RFC 8310) is REQUIRED, and cleartext connections are not permissible. TLS aims to give confidentiality, integrity protection, authentication and anti-replay protection. Servers may also require client certificates.

TLS alone is not complete security: the server name is learned from an SRV query, so a subverted SRV answer could lead to a rogue server. DNSSEC is RECOMMENDED, and the server connection SHOULD be authenticated with DANE TLSA records (RFC 7673), using SNI for the authenticated target name.

SUBSCRIBE is permitted in TLS early data, which can save a round trip, but early data is not forward secret and gives no replay guarantees between connections. Spurious replayed subscriptions create only small, short-lived server state, and servers MAY rate-limit them. TLS session resumption is allowed, but the resumed session starts without subscription state, so the client must resubscribe.
sections.eli5: All the notes travel in a locked box, and you double-check the doorbell is really yours, so nobody can fake a ring.

viz.caption: WHAT THE TTL OF A PUSH CHANGE NOTIFICATION MEANS

items.label: Add record
items.desc: Adds the record with this name, type, class and RDATA; TTL 0 keeps it only while subscribed.

items.label: Remove record
items.desc: Removes the one record given by name, type, class and RDATA.

items.label: Collective remove
items.desc: RDLEN must be zero; removes an RRset, or all RRsets in a class, or in all classes.

items.label: REFUSED
items.desc: Refused for policy or security reasons.

items.label: NOTAUTH
items.desc: Server is not authoritative for the name.
